terms.short: A tiny slice of ownership in one company.
terms.long: Owning one share means you own a small piece of the company. If the company grows its profits, people pay more for each piece, so the price rises. If it struggles, the price falls.

terms.short: One share that holds a whole basket of companies.
terms.long: An exchange-traded fund buys many stocks for you. When you buy one share of the ETF you own a little of everything inside it. Its price is a weighted average of what it holds.

terms.short: Spreading money so one bad event can't sink you.
terms.long: If you own ten unrelated companies and one has a disaster, you lose a tenth at most. Diversification lowers the swings of your portfolio without necessarily lowering the average return. It is the closest thing to a free lunch in investing.

terms.short: A group of companies in the same kind of business.
terms.long: Tech, Energy, Consumer, Finance and Healthcare companies react differently to news. Oil prices matter to energy companies; interest rates matter to banks. Owning several sectors is real diversification; owning ten tech stocks is not.

terms.short: A fund that simply holds the whole market.
terms.long: Instead of picking winners, an index fund buys everything in proportion to its size. MKT100 is our index fund. Over long periods most professional stock pickers fail to beat one, mostly because of fees.

terms.short: A long stretch of rising prices and optimism.
terms.long: Named after a bull thrusting its horns upward. Bull markets usually last years in real life and much longer than bear markets. In TradeSim the market secretly switches between moods; you only find out for sure afterwards.

terms.short: A fall of 20% or more from the last peak.
terms.long: Named after a bear swiping its paws downward. Fear spreads, prices drift lower with bigger swings, and rallies fade. They are painful but historically every one has ended.

terms.short: A sudden, very steep fall over a few days.
terms.long: Panic selling feeds on itself: prices fall, people sell to stop the pain, prices fall more. Crashes are rare and usually short, and wild rebounds often follow. Selling at the bottom locks in the loss.

terms.short: How much a price typically swings each day.
terms.long: We measure it as the standard deviation of daily returns. A stock with 3% volatility often moves ±3% in a day; one with 1% is calm. Higher volatility means a bumpier ride and a bigger chance of a large loss at the wrong moment.

terms.short: How far you fell from your highest point.
terms.long: If your portfolio peaked at $11,000 and is now $9,900, your drawdown is 10%. The maximum drawdown is the worst such fall, the number that tells you how painful an investment felt.

terms.short: How strongly a stock follows the whole market.
terms.long: Beta 1 moves with the market. Beta 1.6 (NVIDIA here) tends to move 60% more: great in a bull market, painful in a crash. Beta 0.5 (Johnson & Johnson) moves about half as much: a 'defensive' stock.

terms.short: A company people buy from in good times and bad.
terms.long: Drinks, groceries and medicine sell even in a recession, so these companies tend to fall less in bear markets and rise less in bull markets. DEF4 holds four of them.

terms.short: A gauge of how stormy the market expects to be.
terms.long: Real markets have the VIX: around 12 when calm, above 30 in a panic. TradeSim's fear gauge is the market's expected yearly swing. Calm days follow calm days and stormy days follow stormy days: volatility clusters.

terms.short: Big moves tend to be followed by more big moves.
terms.long: Markets have memory for storms. After a shock, investors are nervous and react strongly to the next piece of news. TradeSim copies this with a GARCH model, the same idea real risk managers use.

terms.short: The average price over the last N days.
terms.long: A 20-day moving average smooths out daily noise so the trend is easier to see. A price far above its average is 'stretched'. Chart-readers watch when prices cross their averages.

terms.short: The idea that what has been rising keeps rising.
terms.long: Sometimes trends persist because moods persist. But chasing last week's winner often means buying after the good news is already in the price. The What-if Replay tests it.

terms.short: Investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule.
terms.long: Instead of guessing the best day to invest, you invest a slice every week. You automatically buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when they are high, and you never put everything in at the top.

terms.short: What you pay the broker for every trade.
terms.long: A $1 fee looks tiny, but fifty trades cost $50 for certain, whatever happens to prices. Fees are one of the few things in investing you fully control.

terms.short: Profit or loss you locked in by selling.
terms.long: When you sell, the difference between the sale price and what you paid on average becomes real money. Until then it is only on paper.

terms.short: Profit or loss on paper, on shares you still hold.
terms.long: Your NVDA might be up $300 today and down $200 tomorrow. It only becomes realised when you sell.

terms.short: Selling because prices fell, not because anything changed.
terms.long: After a sharp drop it feels safest to get out. But if the company or fund is still sound, selling turns a temporary dip into a permanent loss. Ask: has anything really changed?

terms.short: Whether news is good or bad for a price.
terms.long: Reading sentiment is harder than counting good and bad words: 'not as bad as feared' is good news. Even when you read it right, the headline doesn't say how much the price will move.

terms.short: Letting a computer find a rule from examples.
terms.long: The Robo-analyst is a logistic regression: it learned five weights from thousands of examples by gradient descent. It can spot a stormy market fairly well, but predicting next week's price is barely better than a coin flip. That's true for real markets too.

terms.short: Learning the noise instead of the pattern.
terms.long: A model can memorise the quirks of its training data and look brilliant there, then fail on new data. That's why the Robo-analyst is tested on markets it has never seen.

terms.short: Investing with borrowed money so gains and losses are multiplied.
terms.long: With 2× leverage, $10,000 of your own money buys $20,000 of shares: half yours, half borrowed. If the shares rise 10% you make $2,000 (20% on your money). If they fall 10% you lose $2,000. The loan still has to be paid back whatever happens.

terms.short: A broker account that lends you money to buy shares.
terms.long: Your shares are the security for the loan. The broker charges interest every night and watches your account: if your own money falls too low compared with what you hold, it can sell your shares without asking.

terms.short: The broker's demand to top up, or it sells your shares for you.
terms.long: When your own money (equity) drops below the maintenance level, the broker sells some of your holdings to shrink the loan. It happens after a fall, so you are forced to sell low and miss any rebound. In this game the call comes when you've lost half of your starting cushion.

terms.short: The minimum share of your holdings that must be your own money.
terms.long: US brokers usually require 25%: with $20,000 of shares you must own at least $5,000 of it yourself. The more leverage you use, the closer you start to this line, so a smaller fall crosses it.

terms.short: Selling holdings to pay back a loan, often at the worst time.
terms.long: If a fall wipes out all your own money, the broker sells everything and you may still owe it the difference. With 5× leverage a 20% fall is enough to lose everything you put in.

terms.short: Why a 2× daily fund doesn't give 2× over many days.
terms.long: A fund that resets to 2× every day loses in zig-zags: up 10% then down 10% leaves the market at −1%, but the 2× fund goes +20% then −20%, leaving −4%. Over weeks of chop the gap grows.

terms.short: The waiting buy (bid) and sell (ask) orders at each price.
terms.long: Buyers queue at bid prices below the last trade, sellers at ask prices above it. The gap between the best bid and the best ask is the spread. On the price board, the three best of each side are shown next to every stock.

terms.short: One bar showing a period's open, high, low and close.
terms.long: The thick body runs from the open to the close: green if the price ended higher, red if lower. The thin wicks reach the highest and lowest prices traded. A long lower wick means sellers pushed the price down but buyers fought back.

terms.short: Yesterday's closing price: today's moves are measured from it.
terms.long: On a price board, a price above the reference is shown green, below it red and equal to it yellow. The % change you see all day is against this number.
